title: TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods
summary: TruthfulQA is 817 questions in 38 categories written so that some humans would answer falsely because of misconceptions. The authors distinguish falsehoods caused by not learning the training distribution well (e.g. multiplication errors) from imitative falsehoods, which have high likelihood under the training distribution and are incentivized by the training objective. Under human evaluation the best model (GPT-3-175B with a 'helpful' prompt) is truthful on 58% of questions versus 94% for a human, and larger models are generally less truthful (inverse scaling), while matched control questions improve with size. The authors relate imitative falsehoods to mis-alignment between the imitation objective and users' goals and values, and suggest fine-tuning with objectives other than imitation.
setting: GPT-3 (350M-175B), GPT-Neo/J (125M-6B), GPT-2, UnifiedQA (T5); zero-shot generation with greedy decoding and a multiple-choice variant; human evaluation by the authors plus a fine-tuned GPT-judge; 2021.

quotes.quote: Another possible cause (which doesn't apply to multiplication) is that the model's training objective actually incentivizes a false answer. We call such false answers imitative falsehoods.

We define an answer to a question as truthful iff it avoids asserting a false statement. So truthfulness is consistent with refusing to answer a question, with expressing uncertainty, or with giving a true but irrelevant answer.

Given the current state of research on interpretability, it would be hard to systematically decide whether a language model really "knows" an answer such that it could be generated by the model under different conditions or prompting.
In particular, the questions test a weakness to imitative falsehoods: false statements with high likelihood on the training distribution.
Across all model sizes and prompts, the best model (GPT-3-175B with helpful prompt) produced 58% true answers and 21% true and informative answers.
These are "non-imitative" falsehoods, as they are not incentivized by the model's training objective.
This evidence suggests that the poor performance of models on TruthfulQA is not explained by most questions exploiting a (non-imitative) weakness to a particular syntax or form.
The poor performance of the baseline models is therefore not surprising, as these models are trained to predict human text and do not directly learn to be truthful.

This is an example of mis-alignment between the model's training objective (e.g. to imitate text on the web) and the goals and values of human users (e.g. to avoid offensive language or to avoid falsehoods).
If a model performs well, we cannot conclude that it will be equally truthful on other kinds of tasks (even if we expect some transfer).

key_numbers.quote: The benchmark comprises 817 questions that span 38 categories, including health, law, finance and politics.

key_numbers.claim: Best model versus human, and false-but-informative rate.
key_numbers.quote: This model gave false and informative answers 42% of the time (compared to 6% for the human participant).
For example, the largest GPT-Neo/J is 17% less truthful than a model 60x smaller.
The finetuned GPT-judge model is able to predict human evaluations of truthfulness with 90-96% validation accuracy.

limitations_stated: Questions were adversarially filtered against GPT-3 and may exploit non-imitative weaknesses; reference answers were written by the authors (6-7% disagreement in validation); the benchmark covers short general-knowledge questions, not long-form or interactive settings; good performance does not imply truthfulness on other tasks; a model 'knowing' an answer is not assessed.
open_questions: Whether more diverse or larger models produce the same falsehoods; whether fine-tuning for truthfulness (demonstrations, RLHF, retrieval) closes the gap; how to tell whether a model knows the truth it fails to state.
sense_of_alignment: Uses 'mis-alignment' for a mismatch between the model's training objective (imitating web text) and the goals and values of human users, and says a benchmark is useful 'even when the foundation model is misaligned'. Alignment here is about the training objective, not about what the model tries to do.
